checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one, and work in a level that has a Nav Mesh Bounds Volume. Enable the StateTree and GameplayStateTree plugins. Make a Blueprint named BP_Patroller, a copy of the Third Person character with no input and with a StateTree component. Create a State Tree named ST_Patroller with the StateTreeComponentSchema, and set its Context Actor Class to BP_Patroller.
Add two State Tree Parameters: WaitTime, a float with the value 2.0, and PatrolRadius, a float with the value 800.0.

Create a task named STT_AlertLevel with the parent StateTreeTaskBlueprintBase, and give it an integer variable AlertLevel in the category Output. On Tick, set it to 1 when the player is closer than 1000 units, and to 0 otherwise. Add the task to the Global Tasks of the tree, so it runs the whole time.

Build the states. Under Root, add Calm with the children PickPoint, Walk and Wait, and add a second state named Alert. PickPoint runs a task that outputs a random reachable point using PatrolRadius. Walk moves to that point, so bind its input to the output of the PickPoint task. Wait uses a Delay bound to WaitTime. Link the three with Next transitions so that they loop.

Give Alert an Enter Condition that checks if AlertLevel, bound to the output of the Global Task, is greater or equal to 1. On Calm, add a transition with the trigger On Tick that goes to Alert. In Alert, print Alert and go back to Calm when AlertLevel is 0.
Add failure handling. On Walk, add a transition with the trigger On State Failed that goes to PickPoint, so that a bad point does not stop the loop.
Place three BP_Patroller actors and press Play. Walk close to one of them and watch it switch to Alert and back.

GDQ60.brief: Sight is only one of the senses in the AI Perception system. An enemy can also notice that it was damaged or that something touched it. These senses let an enemy react when the player breaks the rules of stealth, for example by hitting a guard from behind. In this quest you add the damage and touch senses to an enemy and make a sleepy guard wake up when it is hit or touched.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. You need an enemy with an AI Controller that has an AIPerception component with an AI Sight config. If you have none, create an AIController Blueprint named AIC_Enemy with that component, duplicate BP_ThirdPersonCharacter as BP_Enemy, delete its input logic, set its AI Controller Class to AIC_Enemy, and place it in the level. Open the AI Controller. On its AIPerception component, keep AI Sight and add AI Damage and AI Touch to the Senses Config. Give each sense a different Debug Color. Set Dominant Sense to AISense_Sight.
Make the enemy start sleepy: on the AI Sight config, set Starts Enabled to false. Keep Damage and Touch enabled.

On the On Target Perception Updated event, break the AIStimulus. If Successfully Sensed is true, call Set Sense Enabled for AISense_Sight with the value true. Also set a Bool variable named IsAwake to true and store Stimulus Location in a Vector variable named LastStimulus. If your enemy uses a Behavior Tree, store them in Blackboard keys with the same names.
In the player, add a key press that calls Apply Damage on the enemy with any amount. Walk into the enemy to test Touch. Both actions should wake the enemy up.

Open Project Settings, go to AI System, and enable Forget Stale Actors. On the AI Damage config, set Max Age to 5, so that a hit is forgotten after five seconds. Use Get Known Perceived Actors with AISense_Damage to check if the enemy still remembers the hit.
Press Play, then press the apostrophe key and then Numpad 4. Hit the enemy and watch the damage stimulus appear in the color of its sense.

GDQ61.brief: The Gameplay Debugger is a tool that draws information about an AI character on top of the running game. It shows which Behavior Tree branch is active and what the Blackboard values are. Most AI problems come from one wrong Blackboard value, and this tool shows it with one key press. In this quest you use the debugger on an enemy to find a value that blocks a branch.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. You need an enemy that has an AI Controller running a Behavior Tree with a Blackboard. If you have none, follow Epic's Behavior Tree Quick Start Guide, which builds an enemy that patrols and chases the player. Play in the editor. Point the camera at the enemy and press the apostrophe key to select it for debugging.
Press Numpad 1. Read the AI category: Controller Name, Pawn Name, Movement Mode, Behavior (Tree) and Active task. Write them down.
Press Numpad 2. Read the Behavior Tree branch on the left and the Blackboard keys and values on the right. Find one Blackboard key whose value blocks a branch that you expected to run.
Open the Behavior Tree asset and add a breakpoint on one Task node. Play again and note when the game pauses.
Press Numpad 0 to see the NavMesh around the enemy. Then open the console and try the command show Navigation true, and after that show Navigation false.

Stop the game and use Simulate, not Play. Turn the debugger on there as well: press the apostrophe key, or, as the documentation page describes for older versions, enable the Debug AI show flag in the Show menu of the viewport. Select the enemy and switch the categories on and off with the Numpad keys.
Change one tuning value, such as Sight Radius or a chase speed. Play again and confirm the change in the debugger.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Make a new Basic level. Scale the Floor to X 100, Y 100 and Z 1.

Open Project Settings and go to Navigation System. Enable Generate Navigation Only Around Navigation Invokers, and set Invokers Maximum Distance from Seed to 30000. Then go to Navigation Mesh, find Runtime, and set Runtime Generation to Dynamic.
Add a NavMeshBoundsVolume on the floor and scale it to X 500, Y 500 and Z 10.

Copy BP_ThirdPersonCharacter into a folder named NavigationSystem and name the copy BP_NPC_Invoker. Delete its input nodes. Add an event named MoveNPC that calls Get Random Reachable Point In Radius with 1000 from the actor location, and then AI Move To for self. On success, add a Delay of 4 and call MoveNPC again. On fail, add a Delay of 0.1 and call MoveNPC again. Call MoveNPC on Begin Play.
Add a Navigation Invoker component to the Blueprint. Set Tile Generation Radius to 3000 and Tile Removal Radius to 5000. Compile and save.
Place several BP_NPC_Invoker actors in the level and use Simulate. Press P to see the NavMesh tiles, which appear only around each NPC.
Change the two radii to 1000 and 2000 and use Simulate again. Add a Print String on the On Fail path and note how often it runs.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one, and work in a level that has a Nav Mesh Bounds Volume. Enable the SmartObjects and GameplayBehaviors plugins. In Project Settings, under GameplayTags, add the tags SO.Activity.Rest and Character.Type.Villager. Create a Smart Object Definition named SOD_Bench with two Slots. Add the Activity Tag SO.Activity.Rest. Add a user tag query that requires the tag Character.Type.Villager.
Give Slot 0 its own Behavior Definition (a Gameplay Behavior), and leave Slot 1 on the default Behavior Definitions list. Note which one overrides the other.

Create an Actor Blueprint named BP_Bench with a Static Mesh, and add a SmartObject component that points to SOD_Bench. Place two benches in the level. Also add a SmartObject Persistent Collection actor to the level.

Create BP_Villager, a copy of the Third Person character with no input and with the Gameplay Tag Character.Type.Villager. On Begin Play, find Smart Objects around the actor that have the Rest activity tag, and claim one result. Get the slot location from the claim handle and use AI Move To to walk there. Then call Use, add a Delay of 3, and call Release.

Place three BP_Villager actors and one BP_Guard, which is a copy of BP_Villager that runs the same search but does not have the Villager tag. Press Play and watch the slot rings. Two villagers occupy the slots, the third finds no free slot, and the guard finds nothing.
Add a key press that destroys one bench during play. In the villager, bind to the slot invalidated event and print a message when it runs.

GDQ64.brief: In a Mass crowd, avoidance is the steering logic that keeps each agent from walking into walls and into other agents. When it is tuned badly, the crowd gets stuck in narrow places such as a doorway. In this quest you send a crowd through a narrow gap, look at the avoidance data in two debug tools, change the avoidance settings, and compare the result.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. You need a Mass crowd. If you have none, build it first: enable the MassEntity, MassGameplay and MassCrowd plugins and restart the editor, add a large floor with a NavMeshBoundsVolume, create a Mass Entity Config asset named DA_Crowd_Walker with traits for movement, avoidance and visualization (with a simple Static Mesh), and place a MassSpawner with DA_Crowd_Walker, a Count of 200 and an EQS SpawnPoints Generator under Spawn Data Generators.
Build a corridor from two long wall meshes with a gap of about 300 units between them, so that the crowd must squeeze through.

Open Tools > Debug > Visual Logger and select the MassSimulationSubsystem track. In Editor Preferences, under Visual Logger, enable Stick to Recent Data. In the console, run the command ai.debug.mass.SetDebugEntityRange for a few entities, and then use Simulate.
Look at the categories LogAvoidance, LogAvoidanceVelocity and LogAvoidanceAgents. Find the obstacle edges and the predicted collisions near the gap.
Press Play. Press the apostrophe key to open the Gameplay Debugger. Then press Shift+O for the Entity Overview and Shift+V for the avoidance view. Take a screenshot at the gap.

In the avoidance trait of DA_Crowd_Walker, change the moving avoidance parameters, for example the separation settings. Use Simulate again and compare how the crowd flows through the gap. Note the value of stat fps before and after.
Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Read the sections Data Curves, Curve Tables and Data Hookup of the Data Driven Gameplay Elements page that is linked on this quest.

Make a table in a spreadsheet. The header of the first column is Name. The next headers are 0, 1, 2 and 3, which stand for the player level. Add the rows Melee_Damage, Melee_KnockBack and Melee_StunTime with values that grow with each level. Save the table as CT_Combat.csv.
In the Content Browser, click Import and pick the CSV file. Choose Import As CurveTable and the interpolation Linear. Open CT_Combat and click the graph button to see all three curves.

Make an Actor Blueprint named BP_Enemy, or open one of your own, and place it in the level. Add a Curve Table Row Handle variable named DamageCurve and make it Instance Editable. Set its CurveTable to CT_Combat and its RowName to Melee_Damage. Also add a Float variable named PlayerLevel.
On Begin Play, evaluate the row with PlayerLevel and print the result. To find the evaluate node, search for Curve Table in the node menu. Test with PlayerLevel set to 1.5 and note the value.
Reimport the CSV file with the interpolation Constant. Play again with level 1.5 and note the value. Write one sentence that says which mode you would use for damage and why.
Change one value in the CSV file in a text editor. Right-click CT_Combat and choose Reimport. Confirm that the graph updates.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Read the Data Registries page that is linked on this quest. Enable the Data Registry plugin under Edit > Plugins in the Gameplay category, and restart the editor.
Open Project Settings, go to Game, then Data Registry, and add /Game/DataRegistries to Directories to Scan. Create that folder in the Content Browser.

Make the data that the registry will read, if you do not have it yet: a Structure named S_EnemyStats with the float variables Health, Speed and Damage, and a Data Table named DT_Enemies with this row type and the rows Grunt, Runner and Tank. In the DataRegistries folder, right-click, choose Miscellaneous, then DataRegistry, and name the asset DR_EnemyStats. Set Registry Type to EnemyStats. Set Item Struct to S_EnemyStats.
Add a DataTable Source that points to DT_Enemies, the table with Grunt, Runner and Tank. Click Refresh and check that the Registry Preview tab shows the rows.

Make a Data Table named DT_Enemies_Hard that has only the row Grunt, with a higher Health. Add it as a second DataTable Source and drag it ABOVE the first one. Click Refresh and look at Runtime Sources to see both Grunt entries and which one is first.

Make an Actor Blueprint named BP_Enemy, or open one of your own, and place it in the level. Add a Data Registry Id variable. Pick EnemyStats and the row Grunt from the dropdown. On Begin Play, call Acquire Data Registry Item. In its callback, read the item from the cache with the Get Data Registry Item node, and print Health.
Press Play and confirm that Grunt uses the Hard value. Then move DT_Enemies_Hard below DT_Enemies, click Refresh, play again, and confirm that Grunt uses the normal value.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Read the Gameplay Tags page that is linked on this quest. Pay special attention to the parts Defining Gameplay Tags, Gameplay Tag Queries and Setting Tag Editing Restrictions.
Open Project Settings, go to Project, then GameplayTags, and enable Import Tags From Config. Click Add new Gameplay Tag source and name it Combat.ini.
Open Manage Gameplay Tags. Add the tags Damage.Fire, Damage.Ice and Damage.Physical. Give each one a Comment and set its Source to Combat.ini.

Make a Data Table named DT_LootTags with the row type GameplayTagTableRow. Add the rows Loot.Common, Loot.Rare and Loot.Epic. In Project Settings, add the table to Gameplay Tag Table List. Then open the Tag Manager and try to rename Loot.Rare. Note what happens.

Add the tag Status.Wet in the Tag Manager. Make an Actor Blueprint named BP_Enemy, or open one of your own, and give it a Gameplay Tag Container variable named Tags and a Gameplay Tag Query variable named ImmuneQuery. Use the root expression All Expressions Match with two sub-expressions: Any Tags Match with Damage.Fire, and No Tags Match with Status.Wet. Add a function named TakeTaggedDamage that checks the query against a container of incoming tags and skips the damage when it matches.
Test both cases in Play In Editor: call the function once with Damage.Fire alone and once with Damage.Fire and Status.Wet, and print the result of the query each time.
Close the editor. Open the file Config/Tags/Combat.ini in a text editor and add the tag Damage.Poison by hand. Start the editor again and confirm that the tag appears.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Read the Data Assets page that is linked on this quest. Pay special attention to the notes on Data Only Blueprint Classes and Primary Data Asset types.
Make a Blueprint Class named PDA_Weapon with the parent PrimaryDataAsset. Add the variables DisplayName (Text), Damage (Float), FireRate (Float) and Range (Float).
Make a child Blueprint Class named BP_Weapon_Rifle with the parent PDA_Weapon. Do not add any graph nodes, and only set values in Class Defaults. This is a Data Only Blueprint.
Make a Blueprint named BP_Weapon_Rifle_Gold with the parent BP_Weapon_Rifle. Change only Damage, and leave the other values as they are inherited.
Change FireRate in BP_Weapon_Rifle. Then open BP_Weapon_Rifle_Gold and confirm that it has the new FireRate, although you did not edit it.

Now make a Data Asset instance. In the Content Browser, choose Miscellaneous, then Data Asset, pick the class PDA_Weapon, and name the asset DA_Weapon_Pistol. Change a default value in PDA_Weapon and note whether DA_Weapon_Pistol updates.
Write 3 sentences that say when a Data Only Blueprint child is better than a Data Asset instance, and what PrimaryAssetType your Rifle variants have and why.
Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Read the Configuration Files page that is linked on this quest, and look at the parts Syntax, Arrays and Hierarchy.

Make an Actor Blueprint named BP_Tuning in /Game/Blueprints. Add a Float variable EnemyDamageMult with the default 1.0 and an Integer variable StartingLives with the default 3. For each one, expand the advanced variable properties and enable Config Variable.

Close the editor. Open the file Config/DefaultEngine.ini of your project and add a section named [/Game/Blueprints/BP_Tuning.BP_Tuning_C] with the lines EnemyDamageMult=1.5 and StartingLives=5. Add a comment line that starts with ; and explains the values. (Actors read the Engine category.)
Start the editor and place BP_Tuning in the level. Print both values on Begin Play and confirm that the values from the config file are used.

Add a String array variable named BannedWeapons with Config Variable on. In the same section, write these three lines: +BannedWeapons=Rocket, +BannedWeapons=Rocket and .BannedWeapons=Rocket. Print the length of the array, and compare the result with the array example on the page.
Make a file named Config/Windows/WindowsEngine.ini with the same section and the line EnemyDamageMult=2.0. Restart the editor and confirm that the platform file wins over DefaultEngine.ini.
Write 2 sentences that answer this: when would you put a tuning value in a config file and not in a Data Table?
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Read the Blueprint tab of the page Saving and Loading Your Game that is linked on this quest.

Make BP_ProfileSave with the parent SaveGame and the variables Difficulty (Name), TotalKills (Integer) and UnlockedLevels (Name array). Make BP_RunSave with the parent SaveGame and the variables Checkpoint (Name), Health (Float) and Inventory (Name array). Give each class a default slot name: Profile and Run.

Make a Blueprint named BP_SaveGameInstance from the Game Instance class and set it as the Game Instance class in Project Settings, under Maps and Modes. In it, keep a profile object and a run object, and add an event named AddKill that adds 1 to TotalKills in the profile object and calls Async Save Game To Slot. From the Completed pin, print the Success value. To stand in for a kill, add a key press on the character that calls AddKill.

Add a second key press that stands in for reaching a checkpoint. When it is pressed, fill BP_RunSave and save it with Save Game To Slot, the synchronous node that makes the game wait until the save is done. Write 1 sentence that says why a synchronous save is acceptable here or why it is not.
Add a third key press for New Game. It calls Delete Game in Slot for the Run slot only. Use Does Save Game Exist to confirm that the profile file is still there.
On Begin Play, call Async Load Game From Slot for both slots. Cast each result and print Difficulty, TotalKills and Checkpoint. Use the Success pin to handle a missing Run file without an error.
Play: get 3 kills, reach a checkpoint, start a new game, then quit and play again. Look in the Saved/SaveGames folder and confirm that both .sav files are there.
